ABSTRACT: We prove that every coloring of the Euclidean plane with five colors has a monochromatic unit-distance pair, with no regularity assumption on the color classes. Consequently, the chromatic number of the plane is either six or seven.
MAIN STATEMENTS: The extracted interface cycle cannot have length five. | The extracted interface cycle cannot have length four. | The extracted interface cycle cannot have length three.
PROOF OVERVIEW AND THE ROLE OF EARLIER METHODS: The two parts of the proof address different obstacles. A coloring with arbitrary classes provides no density-point structure to use, while a measurable coloring may have boundaries far too irregular to analyze as a planar map. Theorem~ supplies the measurable input. The proof of Theorem~ then constructs the connected interfaces it needs instead of assuming them. Figure~ shows how these two parts combine. \paragraph{From arbitrary labels to measurable fields.} Let $F$ be the field of real algebraic numbers, $E=F(i)$ the algebraic plane, and $K=\{u\in E:|u|=1\}$ its group of algebraic rotations. Restricting a proper coloring to the countable set $E$ and averaging its translates and rotations gives an invariant probability law on proper labelings of $E$. This is a standard amenable averaging construction. Probabilistic approaches to the Hadwiger--Nelson problem already use invariant randomization and finite-graph compactness \citep{BourgeatHeinrichMelottiRobert2015,GwynStavrianos2020}; F\o lner averaging over countable groups of plane isometries also occurs in the fractional-coloring work of \citet{MatolcsiRuzsaVargaZsamboki2025}. These methods supply symmetry. Here a further argument must retain the unit-distance exclusions while producing ordinary measurable functions on the plane. For this purpose let $D$ be the compact group of all characters of the additive discrete group $E$. A character is a homomorphism from $E$ to the unit complex circle. The ordinary continuous characters form the Borel subgroup \[ C=\{z\mapsto\exp(i\xi\cdot z):\xi\in\R^2\}\subset D. \] Rotations act on characters by $(ud)(z)=d(uz)$.
